content.text: In a job market with hundreds of applicants for one post, how can you make sure that you stand out? By writing a good CV and cover letter? Not anymore. Nowadays, many job searches happen through vanous agency websites. The problem with these is that they want your information presented in a way that they can process, which means lots of time spent typing. Another change is that you also need to become your own brand with a constant presence, effectively making your printed list of previous employers and skills redundant

content.text: In today's workplace, many employees fret that their position could be made redundant as a result of employers adopting artificial intelligence (AI), yet there are many reasons that companies may adopt AI, aside from cutting staffing costs. Recent research has found that, while some business leaders are chiefly interested in using AI as a cost-cutting measure, the majority are primarily attracted to AI as a means for increasing efficiency, and thereby gaining a competitive advantage in the market. Other business leaders, meanwhile, were found to express a strong interest in using AI without any specific purpose for doing so. They seemed to want to follow the trend but didn't know exactly how doing so would actually benefit them. Other than fear of redundancy, some workers are resistant to the use of AI because they feel it undermines their professional identity. In roles where expertise is considered of particular importance, workers may feel that the use of AI, due to its ability to rapidly process complex data, diminishes their value to their employer. Nevertheless, despite these concerns, AI seems here to stay within the workplace. For this reason, it is highly advisable for workers to take proactive steps to ensure they can navigate and adapt to the changes it brings. Rather than viewing AI as a threat, they should see it as a tool - one that, for some at least, can lead to professional success.

content.text: Working from home has become more common in a relatively short space of time and has altered many aspects of life, including the family dynamic. Indeed, working parents are now able to be present at home in a way that would have been impossible a few years ago. The shift in how we work has also highlighted just how much money and time were spent on travelling to and from the family home to the office every day, taking large amounts out of often modest salaries. This has led workers to ask - if it's possible to save a fortune on transport costs and work comfortably, maybe it's also possible to work a four-day week? A shorter working week would of course need to be considered carefully by employers. Interestingly, research has indicated that working in this way, employees would be smarter in how they complete their tasks, with the end result being better and faster output. Those not used to this rapid pace of work would potentially burn out, though, which could lead to more sick days being taken and an overly relaxed company culture being unintentionally developed. A four-day week is, at first sight, appealing for both parties. Before any changes could be implemented, however, experts responsible for some of the many research papers on this subject would need to be consulted. There is also the human side to consider. Deep down, many people are resistant to change and enjoy the interaction with colleagues that a normal working week gives them, so they may ultimately be unwilling to change how they work.
